lines.text: With regard to neutrophils, the polymorphonuclear leucocytes, which statement is true?
The answer is: they have a lifespan of only a few hours in inflamed tissue.
Meet the neutrophils, brave little soldiers rushing into the inflamed tissue.
But look at the hourglass beside them. Their time runs out fast.
In an inflammatory lesion, a neutrophil lives only a few hours, and sometimes less.
(sigh) So a severe local infection quickly becomes a graveyard of thousands of neutrophils.
As they fall, their contents, especially their enzymes, spill out and may cause additional damage to host tissues.
Remember: neutrophils have a lifespan of only a few hours in inflamed tissue.
With regard to the microcirculation and the formation of lymph, which statement is true?
The answer is: interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure is normally negative.
Here is the microcirculation, with little drops of fluid leaking out of the blood vessel.
The fluid drips into the interstitial spaces between the cells.
Now the lymphatic opens its mouth and sucks the fluid back, returning it to the circulation.
That suction pulls the gauge below zero. Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure is normally subatmospheric, or negative.
This keeps the tissues structurally intact and the interstitial spaces small.
And small spaces mean short distances for diffusion.
Remember: lymphatic suction makes interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure normally negative.
